The Historical Transition from Coal to Hydrocarbons: Previous Explanations and the Need for an Integrative Perspective1 | Canadian Journal of History

# The Historical Transition from Coal to Hydrocarbons: Previous Explanations and the Need for an Integrative Perspective 1 

Authors: Odinn Melsted and Irene Pallua Author information and affiliations

## Abstract

### Abstract

The article deals with the historical transition from coal to oil and natural gas, commonly referred to as hydrocarbons. This transition occurred throughout the industrialized world between the 1940s and 1970s, yet the causes for the shift from coal to hydrocarbons are only marginally understood. Drawing from recent research on historical energy transitions, we examine the takeover of hydrocarbons in the context of the incumbent coal configurations. Building on previous explanations, we identify two analytical perspectives: (1) the view on the overall energy supply system that diversified when hydrocarbons were introduced, and (2) that on the consumers of energy, who replaced coal with hydrocarbon alternatives. The central argument is that the two perspectives need to be integrated to fully understand why hydrocarbons could replace coal. This monumental change in energy history was no simple shift in fuels, but a complex transition that occurred at (1) the level of energy supply, where hydrocarbons became available as alternatives to coal, and (2) the level of energy consumption, where consumers in the areas of railway and maritime transportation, residential heating, industrial production, and electricity generation actively decided to use hydrocarbon alternatives as substitutions for coal.

### Résumé

Le présent article porte sur la transition énergétique du charbon vers le pétrole et le gaz naturel, généralement appelés hydrocarbures. Cette transition a eu lieu partout dans le monde industrialisé entre les années 1940 et les années 1970; pourtant les causes de cette transition ne sont que très peu comprises. Faisant fond des travaux de recherche récents sur les transitions énergétiques historiques, nous examinons la relève des hybrocarbures dans le contexte des configurations du charbon en place. En nous appuyant sur des explications antérieures, nous identifions deux conceptions analytiques: (1) la première portant sur l’ensemble du système d’approvisionnement énergétique qui s’est diversifié lorsque les hybrocarbures furent introduites, et (2) celle relative aux consommateurs d’énergie, qui remplacèrent le charbon par des solutions alternatives fondées sur les hydrocarbures. L’argument central est que ces deux conceptions doivent être intégrées afin de mieux comprendre la raison pour laquelle les hydrocarbures ont pu remplacer le charbon. Ce changement monumental dans l’histoire de l’énergie ne fut pas un simple changement dans le secteur des combustibles, mais une transition complexe qui eut lieu (1) au niveau de l’approvisionnement en énergie, où les hydrocarbures devinrent disponibles en tant que sources d’énergie alternatives au charbon, et (2) au niveau de la consommation énergétique, où des consommateurs des secteurs ferroviaires et du transport maritime, du chauffage résidentiel, de la production industrielle, ainsi que de la production électrique décidèrent activement d’utiliser les hydrocarbures comme alternative au charbon.

## I. Introduction

Today the world faces a multitude of challenges related to the use of fossil fuels. Environmental pollution, the reality of anthropogenic climate change, and the potential depletion of the world’s fossil fuel resources have induced policy-makers to draft ambitious plans for transitions to renewable alternatives. The main aim is decarbonization, which requires a radical cut in the consumption of fossil fuels. Since the second half of the twentieth century, however, lifestyles in industrialized nations have depended heavily on the excessive consumption of hydrocarbon resources (oil and natural gas). Or as Daniel Yergin puts it in his award-winning book on the history of oil: it has been the era of “Hydrocarbon Man.” 2 From a historical perspective, the rise of “Hydrocarbon Man” also meant the end of “King Coal.” Within a relatively short period of time in the mid twentieth century, coal-based energy solutions were largely replaced with hydrocarbon alternatives. In terms of relative shares in primary energy supply in oecd countries, coal went from sixty-two percent in 1940 to twenty-three percent in 1970, while those of hydrocarbons (oil and natural gas) increased from twenty-six percent to almost seventy percent (Figure 1, see 397 hereafter).

While much has been written on the rise of oil and gas, it is often overlooked that hydrocarbon energy solutions replaced the existing coal-related technologies and practices, such as coal ovens and steam engines. Recent studies on historical transitions have also emphasized that incumbent energy systems, which coal was at the time, tend to be resistant to change. 3 How can the rapid takeover of hydrocarbons be explained? Some causal explanations have been suggested, albeit often as a side-note in macro-oriented studies or as the obligatory “historical background” to histories of oil and gas. The shift is normally explained with the material and economic advantages of hydrocarbons, because their physical properties permit more convenient transport and storage, while their higher energy density enabled an increase in economic efficiency. It has also been pointed out that the post-war hydrocarbon boom was driven by the discovery and development of large oil and gas fields, pricing to compete with coal, as well as innovation in oil-and gas-related technologies. 4 

We see two problems with the existing literature on the transition from coal to hydrocarbons. For one, the number of causal explanations provided in the vast literature on energy history is disparate and difficult to grasp due to the number of sources and variety of research. 5 We consider it necessary to provide an overview to put the existing explanations in a new context by framing the shift from coal to oil and gas as the over-arching transition from coal to hydrocarbons, since we regard the histories of oil and gas as deeply intertwined. By doing so, we do not aim to provide a comprehensive or global overview of the transition from coal to hydrocarbons. Instead, we focus on causal explanations for the general substitution of coal with hydrocarbon alternatives. Our geographical focus lies on Western Europe and the United States, where coal used to be the dominant fuel but was widely replaced with hydrocarbons between the 1940s and 1970s.

The second problem we seek to resolve is the gap between the energy “supply” and “consumption” perspectives. The supply perspective focuses on the diversification of the overall energy supply system once oil and natural gas were introduced to formerly coal-dominated energy economies. The consumption perspective focuses on how individual consumers decided to switch from coal to hydrocarbon alternatives depending on the complexities of the energy economy. The gap between those two perspectives is in many ways a product of the dispersity of historical research on coal, oil, and natural gas, which has tended to focus either on one of these energy carriers specifically or adopt a single perspective on the overall energy economy. Both perspectives provide crucial insights on the causes for the transition. For this reason, we aim to bridge this gap between the “supply” and “consumption” perspective with an integrative perspective.

We argue that the transition from coal to hydrocarbons cannot be fully understood if reduced to one of those perspectives and propose using an integrative perspective, in which these two approaches are connected. This allows us to understand the shift from coal to hydrocarbons as what it really was: a complex transition that occurred both at the level of energy supply, where oil and natural gas became available as alternatives to coal; and at the level of energy consumption, where consumers in the areas of railway and maritime transportation, residential heating, industrial production, and electricity generation actively decided to use hydrocarbon alternatives as substitutions for coal.

## II. Setting the Stage: The Incumbent Configurations of Coal

Studies that offer an overview of the history of oil and natural gas tend to focus on the rise of these fuels during the twentieth century without necessarily examining the connection to pre-existing coal-related technologies, infrastructures, and practices that needed to be altered or replaced. 6 The history of oil, for instance, is often traced to the origins of petroleum refining in the nineteenth century and portrayed as the story of a superior fuel that was bound to take over from coal sooner or later. A well-known example of such a tale is how Winston Churchill, then Minister of War, was convinced by experts that oil would be the better fuel for the Royal Navy’s operations in World War I. Even though Churchill was hesitant to begin with, he is widely acknowledged to have foreseen the future importance of oil. 7 What is not highlighted as much is that only part of the Royal Navy’s fleet were converted to oil, and that it was no radical shift in technology, as the steam ships were merely equipped with oil burners. The majority of British ships continued to use coal, and British ship operators were actually later than others to adopt oil-fired combustion engines as the primary form of marine propulsion. 8 This exemplifies that even though oil was considered a superior fuel, it did not mean it would replace coal immediately or inevitably. Churchill’s decision cannot be assumed to be the decisive event that marked the origins of oil’s triumph in the twentieth century. It was only one of many episodes in the history of the transition from coal to hydrocarbons.

To understand the rise of hydrocarbons, it is essential to examine the circumstances in which they emerged. Coal was more than just a precursor to oil and gas. It was the fuel of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries and the backbone of industrial society; it was used for steam-powered transportation by rail and at sea, for residential heating, industrial production as well as electricity generation. 9 When hydrocarbons started challenging coal’s leading role in the energy mix in the early 1950s, coal was not in recession. On the contrary, coal consumption reached a new peak of thirty exajoules in 1951, and that number remained stable for years to come (Figure 1).

As mentioned, recent studies of historical energy transitions have highlighted that incumbent energy systems tend to be resistant to change. They establish certain configurations of energy production, distribution, and consumption that gain stability. Historians of technology such as Thomas P. Hughes have analyzed these phenomena as technological lock-ins, path dependencies, and technological momentum, which help established technologies to maintain their dominance. 10 Transition researchers work with the concept of incumbent socio-technical regimes, a set of rules that make them (dynamically) stable. Historical transitions from one configuration to another have tended to occur gradually over long periods, as they only succeeded when certain issues with the existing configuration provide “windows” of opportunity for a new one to break through. 11
